extracted.intended_audience: clinicians, clinical chemists, medical students and laboratory technicians performing urine analysis (late-19th/early-20th century methods)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory procedures, diagnostic criteria, and reagent preparations for detecting and quantifying urinary constituents (peptones, mucine, sugars, acetone, fats, blood) in clinical urine analysis. Includes preparatory steps, qualitative reactions, quantitative titration (Fehling), and notes on interferences and precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peptones — general characteristics (Peptones / Propeptones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peptones are final products of the breakdown of albuminoids by digestive ferments; propeptones are transformation products preceding peptones and are chemically very similar. Principal distinguishing feature: propeptones precipitate with ammonium sulfate added to saturation, whereas peptones remain in solution under the same conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peptones characterized by incoagulability by heat, great solubility in water and weak alcohol, non-precipitation by nitric acid (contrast with serine and globulin), precipitable cold by Tanret reagent (iodide of mercury and potassium) but re-dissolved by heat or alcohol (unlike albumin). Note potential confusion with propeptones; research of the two groups may be conflated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove albumin prior to peptone testing (Hofmeister method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before searching for peptones, ensure urine is completely free of albumin because albumin itself gives peptone-like reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hofmeister method: To 100 c.c. urine add 2 c.c. concentrated sodium acetate, then add officinal solution of perchloride of iron dropwise until a precipitate forms and a persistent red coloration. Filter, neutralize with caustic soda to a very slight persistent acid reaction, bring to boiling, cool and filter again. Confirm complete removal: addition of a few drops acetic acid then 2–3 drops potassium ferrocyanide should give no reaction. Only then proceed to peptone reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millon reaction for peptones
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative reaction: mix 4–5 c.c. (or 400–500 c.c. in original) of urine with an equal volume of Millon reagent (complex mercury nitrates) and let stand 45–60 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If peptone present, the supernatant above the precipitate becomes rose or cherry-red. Use as a primary screening reaction after albumin removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biuret reaction for peptones (Réaction du Biuret)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add ~15 c.c. urine to a test tube, add 2–3 drops copper sulfate solution, then 10–15 drops of caustic soda solution (1/10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of peptone produces an amethyst-violet coloration. For simplicity, Fehling's liquor may be used (contains necessary copper and alkali), but the two-step method is preferable. If urine concentration of peptones is low, separation is required first (see phosphotungstic precipitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of peptones by phosphotungstic acid (phosphotungstate precipitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sodium phosphotungstate solution to precipitate peptones from filtered urine that is confirmed albumin-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: filter at least ½ liter urine, mix a small part with 1/5 volume HCl (or better acetic), add a little sodium phosphotungstate solution; if clear after 4–5 minutes, no peptone. Otherwise add 1/10 HCl to whole filtered urine and then phosphotungstate until precipitate forms. Collect precipitate immediately on filter(s) to avoid formation of a secondary reddish precipitate. Wash precipitate with water containing 3–5% sulfuric acid until filtrate is colorless, triturate wet with powdered baryta hydrate and a little water, warm 10–15 minutes, filter: filtrate contains peptones for further reactions. If excess baryta hydrate used, neutralize cautiously with dilute sulfuric acid and remove barium sulfate by filtration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tanret (iodide of mercury and potassium) behavior distinguishing peptones from albumin
rubrics_metrics.description: Tanret reagent precipitates peptones cold, similar to albumin, but the precipitate redissolves with heat or alcohol—this does not happen with true albumin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a distinguishing test, but be aware many alkaloids share this reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mucine — properties and detection (Mucine in urine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mucine (constituent of mucus) is a derivative of albuminoid matter, viscous and filamentous, insoluble in water (but swells and appears to dissolve in large volumes). Traces commonly present; increased in febrile and catarrhal affections of urinary mucosa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acetic acid precipitates mucine; excess acetic acid does not redissolve this precipitate (contrast with mineral acids). For notable mucine, addition of excess acetic acid yields a uniform turbidity that persists after filtration; flocs form only rarely. Facilitate flocculation by diluting urine several volumes of water and waiting several hours. For albuminous urine, pre-dilute 1–2 volumes water and, after rest and filtration, check albumin by heat in the clear filtrate before mucine tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of urinary sugars to consider (glucose, lactose, inosite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sugars encountered in urine include glucose (dextrose), lactose (milk sugar), and inosite (muscular sugar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different clinical contexts: glucose typical of diabetes mellitus but may appear transiently after meals or due to nervous lesions or substances. Lactose often present in small amounts in pregnant/nursing women and behaves like glucose in reduction tests; inosite sometimes appears in diabetics and albuminurics but does not reduce Fehling or bismuth tests and is operationally difficult to detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical features suggesting glucosuria
rubrics_metrics.description: Urines in frank diabetes commonly show markedly increased volume (3–4 L/day, sometimes up to 15–20 L), very clear color, high specific gravity (1.030–1.060), and possible white crust on clothing after drying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantity of sugar excreted in 24 hours may vary from a few grams to hundreds of grams; very large amounts reported historically. These clinical signs guide decision to perform sugar tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject KOH boiling test for glucose (avoid Potash boil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation: absolutely avoid the old method of boiling urine with caustic potash to test for sugar; resulting yellow/brown coloration occurs frequently in absence of glucose and requires substantial sugar to be perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Fehling or bismuth-based methods which are more specific and sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fehling's test for sugar (qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fehling (cupro-potassic) solution is a tartrate of copper in excess caustic potash. Heat 3–4 c.c. Fehling to boiling in a test tube; it should remain clear. Add urine dropwise — immediate formation of a precipitate first yellow then red indicates sugar (glucose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sugar amount low, add more urine and re-boil briefly. If no red deposit within ~1 minute, conclude sugar absent. Beware other reducing substances (uric acid, creatinine, xanthine) reduce Fehling but more slowly and less distinctly (green/yellow deposits). Pre-boil Fehling (preferably with a little water) before adding urine to avoid false positives due to spontaneous reduction of old reagent. For albuminous urine, remove albumin first (see albumin removal) because albumin hinders reduction; after acidifying with acetic and boiling and filtering the coagulum, alkalinize filtrate before testing. For decomposed urine containing ammoniacal salts, boil to volatilize ammonia then cool, add excess caustic soda and boil with Fehling to drive off remaining ammonia; if Fehling unchanged, no sugar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interferences in Fehling test — substances producing false positives
rubrics_metrics.description: Several substances when present in urine can reduce Fehling reagent and mimic sugar: glycerin, chloroform, chloral hydrate, turpentine, sodium benzoate, plus endogenous reductants like uric acid, creatinine, xanthine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish by reaction speed and color of precipitate; delayed green/yellow deposits typically not considered positive for glucose. Remove albumin/ammonia and consider complementary tests (bismuth test, dipsticks, titration) when doubt exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bismuth subnitrate test for sugar (sous-nitrate de bismuth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a pinch (0.15–0.20 g) of powdered bismuth subnitrate in a tube, add ~1 c.c. caustic soda, heat slightly (no color change should occur) then add 4–5 c.c. urine and boil with agitation; in presence of sugar the bismuth oxide is reduced to metallic bismuth (black pulverulent precipitate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If very sweet, excess alkali chars sugar to yellow/brown; after settling, expect brown liquid over black bismuth. Urine must be albumin-free; albumin sulfur can produce sulfide blackening of bismuth causing false positives. To avoid errors, mix bismuth powder with caustic first; beware sulfide contaminants in commercial alkalies which can give black bismuth even without sugar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable dip-and-heat reagent strips (indigo + bicarbonate) — qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Portable reagents: two impregnated paper strips (one with indigo, one with concentrated bicarbonate). Dip each into urine; the indigo-colored strip is heated and, if sugar present, decolorizes rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convenient for bedside screening, though the author refrains from endorsing their accuracy conclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dosage of sugar by Fehling titration (quantitative sugar assay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred quantitative method: titrate Fehling's solution with a standard glucose solution. Prepare Fehling freshly: dissolve copper sulfate and prepare tartrate + caustic mixture; final volume 1 L. Ten c.c. Fehling should be reduced by 0.05 g glucose (or titrate to determine actual titre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fix titre: prepare 1 g glucose in 200 c.c. distilled water (so 10 c.c. contains 0.05 g). In a small flask dilute 10 c.c. Fehling to 30 c.c. water, boil, and add glucose solution dropwise via burette until decoloration completes, taking care near endpoint. Filter promptly and verify that diluted Fehling won't give further reduction on heating with sweet solution; note common observed titres (e.g., 10 c.c. Fehling may be reduced by 9.5 c.c. sugar solution equating to 0.0475 g glucose). Recheck titre periodically; prepare small quantities and store protected from light and heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for titrating urine sugar with Fehling (practical dosage in urine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure urine sugar concentration is not too high (>~10 g/L) — dilute if necessary. Filter urine, fill a measured burette, prepare 10 c.c. Fehling diluted to 40 c.c. (10 + 30 water) in a small flask, boil and add urine dropwise according to titration technique described for standardization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volume of urine needed to decolorize corresponds to an amount of glucose (e.g., volume that decolorizes 10 c.c. Fehling equals 0.0470 g glucose under assumed titre); convert to grams per liter taking into account any dilution. If urine contained albumin, remove beforehand by acidifying with acetic and boiling, filter and recombine washes, then dilute urine to double volume before titration and correct calculations accordingly. The author considers this albumin-removal-by-boiling-and-dilution simpler and less error-prone than lead subacetate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarimetric (saccharimetric) method referenced for sugar quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarimetric (saccharimetric) method mentioned as alternative for sugar dosage; author defers details to more specialized treatises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note historical correction: saccharimetric coefficient should be 2.063 (not 2.22) as demonstrated by Grimbert (J. de Ph. et Ch., 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lactose (sugar of milk) — detection considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lactose often appears in small amounts in urine of pregnant/nursing women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lactose behaves like glucose in Fehling and bismuth reduction tests; keep this in mind when interpreting positive reduction results in such patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inosite (muscular sugar) — detection notes and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Inosite is occasionally found in urine of diabetics and albuminuric patients; it does not reduce Fehling or bismuth reagents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection is operationally difficult and of limited practical use to the intended readership; the author merely notes its existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acetone detection — Chautard fuchsine method (qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct color reaction: a fuchsine solution decolorized by sulphurous acid regains color upon addition of acetone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: dissolve 0.05 g fuchsine in 100 c.c. water, bubble sulphurous acid until decolorized (avoid excess), add a few drops to 10–15 c.c. urine. If acetone present, solution turns pink. The reaction is unreliable: small acetone amounts may not react; sometimes urine without acetone restores fuchsine color. Prefer distillation before testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acetone detection by distillation + iodoform (Lieben) — preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Distill 100–150 c.c. urine and collect first 15–20 c.c. (acetone boils ~56°C so concentrates in early distillate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to perform Lieben iodoform test on distillate: add a bit of iodine in potassium iodide and a little caustic potash; depending on acetone amount, iodoform precipitate forms characterized by odor and crystalline form. To reveal crystals, agitate with ether and allow ether evaporation to leave crystalline iodoform. Distillation before reaction reduces false positives and increases sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of fats in urine (lipiduria / chyluria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatty matter is rare in temperate regions but common in hot climates; urine appears milky, forming a white creamy surface layer of fat globules; often albuminous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize fats by: 1) glued paper strip immersed and dried — stain persists; 2) shaking urine with ether which extracts fats and clarifies urine; decant and evaporate ether to residue and re-test paper; 3) microscopic exam often shows fat globules. Differentiate from pus: microscopic exam reveals pus cells, and ether treatment will not clear pus-containing opacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood in urine — recognition and Heller test
rubrics_metrics.description: Urines containing blood range in color from pale pink to dark brown, are turbid, and always contain albumin. Sediment after standing should show numerous erythrocytes on microscopic exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat-filtered urine acidified with acetic acid — yields a coagulum which is brownish when blood products present (contrast to white coagulum without blood). Heller's test: boil a few c.c. urine with caustic soda to strongly alkaline reaction; phosphates precipitate carrying colored blood matter as reddish-brown flakes while supernatant turns bottle-green. Use sediment microscopy (§122 referenced) to confirm hematuria (presence of erythrocytes).
